intro: Trastevere means "across the Tiber," and this district has always lived that way: with its back to the power on the other bank, with its own saints, its own god of medicine, and an island shaped like a ship in the middle of the river. You'll count the sides of Rome's oldest fountain, hunt for a snake carved in stone, and look closely at a saint who has been sleeping in marble for centuries. It's about 3 km, flat, almost always by the water.
puntoPartida: Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere, facing the basilica's façade

paradas.llegada: Stand in Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere, facing the basilica's façade. Look up, just above the columns of the portico: a golden frieze shines up there.
paradas.enigma: That 13th-century mosaic shows the enthroned Virgin nursing the Child. Around her stands a row of women, each holding an oil lamp: two hold theirs unlit, the rest lit. Not counting the Virgin, how many women are there in total?
pistas: They're arranged in a row on both sides of the Virgin, the same number on each side.
It's a number between 8 and 12.
There are ten women.
paradas.historia: No one fully agrees on who these ten women are: the most common reading identifies them with the wise and foolish virgins from a parable in Matthew's Gospel, the ones who carried spare oil for their lamps and the ones who didn't. Local legend adds another oil story: they say that on the night Christ was born, a spring of oil burst from the ground on this very spot and flowed all the way to the Tiber — which is why, for centuries, this church was also known as Santa Maria in Fontibus.
paradas.fuente: Basilica di Santa Maria in Trastevere; Sovraintendenza Capitolina — façade mosaic

paradas.llegada: Turn toward the center of the square, where a travertine stone fountain rises on a set of steps, a little apart from the church façade.
paradas.enigma: This fountain competes with another in Rome for the title of the city's oldest: some trace its origins to the 8th century, though what you see today is the result of at least four rebuilds — Bramante, Bernini, and Carlo Fontana all had a hand in it, each in his own way and century. Look at the large, raised basin, decorated with carved shells at the corners: how many sides does it have?
pistas: It's neither square nor round: it's a regular polygon with more than six sides.
It's the same number of sides as a stop sign.
It has eight sides: it's an octagon.
paradas.historia: Bramante gave it its first shape around 1499; soon after, it became octagonal; Bernini moved it to the exact center of the square and added the large shells in 1659; Carlo Fontana finished it off in 1692, and in 1873 it was rebuilt once again, stone by stone, following that same design. Few fountains in Rome have changed shape so many times without ever changing location.
paradas.fuente: Comune di Roma; Sovraintendenza Capitolina — Fontana di Piazza Santa Maria in Trastevere

paradas.titulo: The Eye that Warns of Floods
paradas.llegada: Leave the square heading north along Via della Scala until you reach Piazza Trilussa, by the river. From there, a pale stone footbridge begins: the Ponte Sisto.
paradas.enigma: This bridge was commissioned by Pope Sixtus IV between 1473 and 1479, built over the ruins of an earlier Roman bridge. Look for a large opening right above the central arch, cutting straight through the bridge from one side to the other — wide enough that you can see the sky through it. Romans affectionately call it the occhialone, "big eye," because for centuries it warned of danger: when the Tiber's water started coming through it, it was time to run. What shape is that opening?
pistas: It has no corners and no straight sides.
It's the same shape as a coin or a wheel.
It's circular: a big circle, the "occhialone."
paradas.historia: Beneath the water, with barely a visible trace, lie the remains of an earlier bridge commissioned by Agrippa before 12 BC. Over the centuries it was also known as the pons Aurelius, until a flood brought it down in the year 791 and it became known as the pons fractus, "broken bridge" — the very same nickname, curiously, carried today by another Roman bridge in this city, downstream, which you'll reach later on this route.
paradas.fuente: Sovraintendenza Capitolina — Ponte Sisto; Touring Club Italiano

paradas.llegada: Backtrack south, following the Lungotevere along the Trastevere bank, to the Ponte Cestio, the three-arched bridge that crosses to Tiber Island (Isola Tiberina). Cross it and look for the tip of the island facing downstream, not far from the church of San Bartolomeo.
paradas.enigma: Since the 1st century BC, Romans have faced this tip of the island with travertine stone to make it look like the prow of a ship, with an obelisk at the island's center standing in for the mast. Legend says that in 291 BC, with Rome ravaged by an epidemic, envoys brought a statue of the god of medicine back from Greece; on the return voyage, the god's sacred snake escaped the ship and swam ashore right here, marking the spot where his temple should be built. On the stone of the prow you can still make out a carved staff with an animal coiled around it. What animal is it?
pistas: It's a legless reptile, the star of this place's founding legend.
It's the same animal that still appears today in the international symbol of medicine.
It's a snake, coiled around the staff of Aesculapius.
paradas.historia: The snake led the Romans to Aesculapius, the Greek god of medicine, who came to Rome to stop the epidemic. The tradition has never been broken: where his temple once stood, there is still a hospital today, the Fatebenefratelli — so this island has been curing people, without a break, for over two thousand years.
paradas.fuente: Sovraintendenza Capitolina — Isola Tiberina; Ospedale Fatebenefratelli

paradas.titulo: The Bridge that Gave Up to the River
paradas.llegada: From the island, look downstream, to the south, toward the next modern bridge, the Ponte Palatino. Just before it, in the middle of the water, there's something that is no longer a whole bridge.
paradas.enigma: In the middle of the river, isolated and connected to neither bank, a single stone arch stands alone: it's all that remains of the Pons Aemilius, Rome's oldest stone bridge, whose arches were finished in 142 BC. Count how many complete arches are still standing today above the water.
pistas: It's not a whole bridge: only one fragment survives, alone in the middle of the river.
It's the smallest possible number that isn't zero.
Only one arch remains.
paradas.historia: Romans call it Ponte Rotto, "broken bridge" — almost the same story that had already happened, centuries earlier, to Ponte Sisto. The great flood of 24 December 1598 swept away three of the six arches the bridge had at the time, and they were never rebuilt. Two more arches disappeared in the late 19th century, when the current embankment walls were built along the Tiber to control flooding, leaving standing only the arch you see today, resting on Roman piers from the 2nd century BC.
paradas.fuente: Sovraintendenza Capitolina — Pons Aemilius (Ponte Rotto); Roma Capitale

paradas.llegada: Head southwest, away from the river, to the Basilica di Santa Cecilia in Trastevere (entry to the church is free). Approach the main altar: below it, in a recess at floor level, there's a white marble sculpture of a woman lying on her side.
paradas.enigma: It was carved by Stefano Maderno in 1600, shortly after Saint Cecilia's tomb was opened and her body was found, so it was said at the time, incorrupt after 1,300 years. Maderno swore he had sculpted the exact position in which he saw her: on her side, her face turned away and hidden, her hands extended in a very specific way. Look at her right hand, the one more clearly visible: how many fingers is it extending?
pistas: It's neither a closed fist nor a fully open hand.
It's a number smaller than five.
It extends three fingers.
paradas.historia: In her other hand, Cecilia extends a single finger: three and one, her silent way of proclaiming the Trinity — one God in three persons — with the final gesture of her life. Cecilia is the patron saint of musicians today because, according to legend, she sang in her heart for God while being forced into marriage; the basilica that houses her is said to stand on the remains of her own house.
paradas.fuente: Basilica di Santa Cecilia in Trastevere; sculpture by Stefano Maderno (1600)

paradas.titulo: The Number that Gives the District Away
paradas.llegada: Head back north, into the heart of Trastevere, to Vicolo del Bologna, one of the district's most photographed little streets: colorful façades, uneven cobblestones, and, almost always, laundry strung from balcony to balcony.
paradas.enigma: Look for the white marble plaque bearing the street name, mounted on one of the walls. Besides the name, Rome's traditional street plaques carry a Roman numeral in one corner: the number of the rione, the historic district the street belongs to — Rome has 22 rioni in total. What Roman numeral appears on this plaque?
pistas: It's a Roman numeral made of an X followed by several I's.
In ordinary numbers, it's 13.
The number is XIII: Trastevere is Rome's 13th rione.
paradas.historia: The official emblem of rione XIII is a golden lion's head on a red background; no one fully agrees on its origin, though one theory links it to the Christians of Trastevere martyred in Roman arenas. Vicolo del Bologna, for its part, owes its name to a 16th-century carpenter nicknamed "il Bologna" — one more of the hundreds of trades and nicknames that Rome has kept, almost without meaning to, in the names of its streets.
paradas.fuente: Roma Capitale — toponomastica e rioni di Roma; Roma Segreta — Vicolo del Bologna

paradas.llegada: Return to Piazza di Santa Maria in Trastevere, once again facing the basilica. This time look at the columned portico beneath the golden mosaic, and look up at the stone balustrade crowning it.
paradas.enigma: This portico was added by the architect Carlo Fontana in 1702. On the balustrade that tops it stand several stone statues, each representing a different pope from the early centuries of the Church. Count them: how many statues of popes are up there?
pistas: They're standing in a row, right above the portico's columns.
It's a number between 2 and 6.
There are four statues of popes.
paradas.historia: They are Callixtus I, Cornelius, Julius I, and Calepodius: popes of the 3rd and 4th centuries, all linked to the founding of this basilica, the first in Rome officially dedicated to the Virgin. This same portico has also housed, since the 18th century, a collection of pagan and Christian tombstones rescued from the Roman catacombs — loose fragments of two thousand years of history, gathered in the very square where you began and ended this route.
paradas.fuente: Basilica di Santa Maria in Trastevere; Sovraintendenza Capitolina — portico di Carlo Fontana (1702)

final.titulo: You've Crossed the River Without Getting Wet
final.texto: From ten mosaic lamps to a bridge that lost every arch but one, from a snake that founded a hospital two thousand years ago to a saint who left her final message in the fingers of one hand. Trastevere always lived with its back to the power on the other bank, with its own saints, its own god, and its own rules — and if you knew how to look, you can still feel it.
